lesson.title: Essen I: der Fisch, das Fleisch, der Käse, die Suppe, das Gemüse
lesson.subtitle: the table's backbone — two sound twins, two Latin guests, and one word English never touched

hook.title: Two Twins and Three Guests at the Table
hook.content: The German table's backbone is five nouns, and they arrive by three different roads. der Fisch ↔ the fish is the easy one: the same Proto-Germanic word, *fiskaz, the same sound in both languages — no badge, no story, just a twin. das Fleisch ↔ the flesh is the same word with a narrowing: English pushed flesh toward the body and handed the table to 'meat', while German kept Fleisch doing both jobs. der Käse and die Suppe are Latin guests: Käse is Latin caseus, and English cheese is the same Latin word that walked in through a different door; Suppe is Late Latin suppa, 'bread soaked in broth' — the word behind both soup and the sop you soak in it, and a Latin word that was itself borrowed from Germanic, so soup left home and came back. das Gemüse is the odd one out: no twin, no Latin — it grew inside German from an old word for soft food (Middle High German gemüese, 'mush, food'), and English never borrowed it, which is why German has to lend it to you now.

footnotes.title: Friday Is Fish Day
footnotes.content: Am Freitag essen wir Fisch is not a textbook sentence — it is a habit. Catholic Germany kept meat off the Friday table for centuries, and the fish custom outlived the rule: der Freitag is still der Fischtag on many German menus. Your new words Essen, Freitag and Fisch ride in one real sentence.

pattern.title: How the Table Words Sit
pattern.content: Four frames, one meal. 1. General food takes no article: Ich esse Fisch, Wir essen Suppe — exactly like English 'we eat soup', the food stands bare. 2. The heat frame: Die Suppe ist sehr heiß — heiß is the heat-word you own from tea, and the food noun keeps its gender (der Fisch, das Fleisch, der Käse, die Suppe, das Gemüse). 3. The festival frame: zu + dative names the occasion — zu Ostern, zu Weihnachten: Zu Ostern essen wir Fisch. 4. The frequency slot: Am Freitag essen wir immer Fisch — immer rides directly behind the conjugated verb, the same slot lesson 5131 drilled, and jetzt parks there too: Ich esse jetzt Suppe.
pattern.linguist_note: English split the old work between two words and narrowed both: meat (once 'any food' — sweetmeats!) became the table word, flesh retreated to the body. German never moved: Fleisch still serves both the butcher and the anatomist. One Proto-Germanic word, two fates.

exercises.prompt: The table's backbone — match each sentence with its reading:

matching_pairs.english: We always eat fish on Friday
matching_pairs.german: Am Freitag essen wir immer Fisch

matching_pairs.english: The cheese on the bread is tasty
matching_pairs.german: Der Käse auf dem Brot ist lecker

matching_pairs.english: I eat fish with fork and knife
matching_pairs.german: Ich esse Fisch mit Gabel und Messer

matching_pairs.english: The coffee is in the mug
The pot stands on the table
matching_pairs.german: Die Kanne steht auf dem Tisch

exercises.target_answer: Am Freitag essen wir immer Fisch, Der Montag ist ein Wochentag, Ich esse Fleisch mit Gemüse, Die Suppe ist sehr heiß, Der Käse auf dem Brot ist lecker, Ich esse Fisch mit Gabel und Messer, Der Kaffee ist im Becher, Die Kanne steht auf dem Tisch, Eine Flasche Wasser, bitte
exercises.meaning: always fish on Friday, weekday, meat with vegetables, hot soup, cheese on bread
exercises.explanation: Five foods in five frames. General food takes no article (Ich esse Fleisch mit Gemüse), and immer sits directly behind the verb — the frequency slot from lesson 5131.

exercises.prompt: Which of these four words did English never take — no twin, no loan, the one that grew inside German alone?
exercises.meaning: das Gemüse = the one English never got
exercises.explanation: Käse and Suppe are Latin loans English shares; Fisch is a pure sound twin. Gemüse grew inside German — Middle High German gemüese, 'soft food, mush' — and English never touched it. The honest odd one out.

exercises.prompt: 'das Fleisch' is the same ancient word as its English twin — but English narrowed it to the body. What is the twin?
exercises.meaning: das Fleisch ↔ flesh: same word, narrower English life
exercises.explanation: Both come from Proto-Germanic *flēską. English pushed flesh to the body and handed the table to 'meat'; German kept Fleisch doing both jobs — the butcher's and the anatomist's.

exercises.prompt: Assemble the festival sentence: 'At Easter we eat fish'
exercises.explanation: zu + dative names the occasion: zu Ostern, zu Weihnachten. The verb holds slot 2 and the food stays bare — no article on Fisch, because it is food in general.
jetzt goes straight behind the conjugated verb — the same slot immer and oft used in lesson 5131. Suppe stands bare because it is food in general, not one specific bowl.

summary.outcome: Name the five table nouns with their genders, eat them in bare-object sentences, and slot immer and jetzt behind the verb.

use_example.german: Zu Ostern essen wir Fisch — am Freitag essen wir immer Fisch.
use_example.english: At Easter we eat fish — on Friday we always eat fish.

summary.takeaway: Fisch and Fleisch are twins (English narrowed Fleisch to flesh), Käse and Suppe are shared Latin loans, Gemüse grew alone in German — and the genders stand: der Fisch, das Fleisch, der Käse, die Suppe, das Gemüse.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: fruit and vegetables — die Kartoffel named after an Italian truffle, die Tomate from Nahuatl, and das Obst, the Latin shelf-label.

twist.prompt: Without looking back — rebuild the core sentence from Essen I: der Fisch, das Fleisch, der Käse, die Suppe, das Gemüse (I am eating soup now):
twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Ich esse jetzt Suppe" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of Essen I: der Fisch, das Fleisch, der Käse, die Suppe, das Gemüse without relying on short-term echo.

fisch.context_translation: The fish swims in the water.

fleisch.context_phrase: Ich esse gern Fleisch mit Kartoffeln.
fleisch.context_translation: I like eating meat with potatoes.
fleisch.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *flaiski — the exact counterpart of English flesh. [wiktionary]

käse.context_phrase: Der Käse auf dem Brot ist lecker.
käse.context_translation: The cheese on the bread is tasty.
käse.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *kāsī, borrowed early from Latin cāseus — shared with English cheese. [wiktionary]

suppe.etymology_derivation: Borrowed via Middle Low German suppe under French influence — both trace to Proto-Germanic *supô 'broth'. [wiktionary]

gemüse.etymology_derivation: From Old High German muos 'food, porridge'; English mush is only a possible cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

immer.context_phrase: Ich trinke immer Kaffee am Morgen.
immer.context_translation: I always drink coffee in the morning.
immer.etymology_derivation: OHG iomēr 'ever + more' — cognate with Middle English 'a mare' (evermore). [wiktionary]

jetzt.etymology_derivation: Old High German iozuo, je (ever) + zu (to); no English cognate — memorize this one. [wiktionary]

ostern.context_translation: We look for Easter eggs at Easter.
ostern.etymology_derivation: From Old High German ōstarūn, from Proto-West Germanic *Austrā; the page compares English Easter — the same Germanic festival name of the dawn-east direction (cf. Osten, east). [wiktionary]

wochentag.context_phrase: Am Wochentag arbeite ich bis fünf.
wochentag.context_translation: On a weekday I work until five.
wochentag.etymology_derivation: Woche + Tag — the exact compound of weekday; both elements are documented twins (week, day). [wiktionary]

gabel.context_phrase: Ich esse den Salat mit der Gabel.
gabel.context_translation: I am eating the salad with the fork.
gabel.etymology_derivation: From West Germanic gabulu, meaning fork; English gable is the same Germanic word, naming the fork-shaped upper end of a house wall. [wiktionary]

messer.context_phrase: Schneide das Brot mit dem Messer.
messer.context_translation: Cut the bread with the knife.
messer.etymology_derivation: From Old High German mezzisahs, literally food knife; the first part is the food root behind English meat, the second the knife root behind English saw, with t appearing as ss in German. [wiktionary]

becher.context_phrase: Ich trinke den Kakao aus einem Becher.
becher.context_translation: I am drinking the cocoa from a mug.
becher.etymology_derivation: From West Germanic bikari, borrowed from Latin bicarium, likely a diminutive of Greek bikos, meaning jar or amphora; English beaker is the same Latin loan. [wiktionary]

kanne.context_phrase: Die Kanne Tee ist noch heiß.
kanne.context_translation: The pot of tea is still hot.
kanne.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic kanno; English can is a direct cognate from Old English canne, originally meaning cup or vessel. [wiktionary]

flasche.context_phrase: Die Flasche Wasser kostet zwei Euro.
flasche.context_translation: The bottle of water costs two euros.
flasche.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic flasko, from a root meaning to plait or braid, since bottles were once wrapped in straw; English flask is a direct cognate. [wiktionary]

essen.shift_rule: T → S / SS / Z + Ablaut Vowels
essen.context_translation: What do we want to eat?
essen.etymology_derivation: Medial t → ss. Noun: das Essen (food).

freitag.etymology_derivation: Frigg's/Freia's day — both languages named the day for the Germanic love goddess, spelled two ways. [wiktionary]

lecker.etymology_derivation: From Middle High German lecker, tied to the verb lecken, to lick, Proto-West Germanic *likkōn; the entry points to English lick as the relative, so the word family is literally about licking. [wiktionary]

brot.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *braudą — originally "the fermented/risen thing", kin to the verb brew (German brauen). Bread is "the brewed thing". [wiktionary]
